kid.question: Who will set up the kingdom that will stand forever?

options.text: The princes of Judah
The rulers of Media
The God of heaven
The king of Babylon

kid.explanation: Daniel says the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed.

kid.question: What did the king say Daniel's God could do?

options.text: Train soldiers
Store grain
Command musicians
Reveal secrets

kid.explanation: The king calls Him a revealer of secrets because Daniel revealed the matter.

kid.question: What did Daniel ask for his three friends?

options.text: Authority to rebuild Jerusalem's temple
Positions overseeing affairs in Babylon
Places serving in the royal army
Permission to settle back in Judah

kid.explanation: At Daniel's request, the king placed his friends over the affairs of the province of Babylon.

kid.question: Why did the king gather the provincial rulers?

options.text: To dedicate his newly made image
To choose his next army captain
To welcome his new foreign bride
To divide his land among governors

kid.explanation: The officials gathered for the dedication of the golden image on the plain of Dura.

kid.question: What signal told the people to bow to the image?

options.text: The opening of the city gates
The rising of the morning sun
The sound of musical instruments
The arrival of the royal guards

kid.explanation: The herald commanded the people to fall down and worship when they heard the instruments.

kid.question: What punishment was announced for refusing to bow?

options.text: Being thrown into a burning furnace
Being sold to a foreign army
Being sent to a distant prison
Being driven into the open desert

kid.explanation: The decree threatened immediate casting into a fiery furnace for refusing worship.

kid.question: Which three men were accused before the king?

options.text: Ezra, Nehemiah, and Zerubbabel
Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego
Hanani, Haggai, and Zechariah
Reuben, Simeon, and Levi

kid.explanation: The accusers named the three men appointed over Babylon's affairs and charged them with refusing the king's worship.

kid.question: What did the three friends say if they were not rescued?

options.text: They would ask for new gods
They would still refuse the image
They would serve the king's priests
They would then bow before it

kid.explanation: They affirm God's power to deliver, yet declare that even if not delivered they will not serve the king's gods or image.

kid.question: What happened to the men who carried the friends toward the furnace?

options.text: The flames killed the king's soldiers
The king rewarded the strongest soldiers
The guards released the three prisoners
The heat drove the soldiers away

kid.explanation: The urgent command and extreme heat led to the flames killing the men who carried them up.

kid.question: What surprised the king when he looked into the fire?

options.text: One man standing beside the doorway
Three men sitting bound and silent
Two men climbing out with ropes
Four men walking free and unharmed

kid.explanation: The king had cast in three bound men but now saw four loose, walking without hurt.

high-school.question: How is God's kingdom contrasted with the preceding kingdoms?

options.text: It survives by joining kingdoms rather than keeping a separate identity
It restores earlier kingdoms rather than bringing their dominion to an end
It endures and consumes kingdoms rather than passing to another people
It divides among later kingdoms rather than ruling as one kingdom

high-school.explanation: The kingdom is never destroyed or left to other people; it breaks and consumes the others and stands forever.

high-school.question: How does the court respond to the revealed secret?

options.text: The king acknowledges God's revealing power and elevates Daniel
The king conceals God's revealing power and appoints a new interpreter
The king disputes God's revealing power and consults the same astrologers
The king dismisses God's revealing power and returns Daniel to captivity

high-school.explanation: Nebuchadnezzar names God a revealer of secrets, honors Daniel, and appoints him to high authority.

high-school.question: What combines to make the image's worship a public imperial demand?

options.text: Gathered merchants, a market summons, taxation, and a trade exemption
Gathered priests, a private covenant, silence, and a voluntary offering
Gathered officials, a multilingual summons, music, and a threatened penalty
Gathered soldiers, a border treaty, fasting, and a temporary ceasefire

high-school.explanation: The dedication includes officials and a command to peoples, nations, and languages, enforced by the furnace penalty.

high-school.question: How do the accusers frame the three men's refusal?

options.text: As an attempt to overthrow the king by rival army commanders
As disagreement over the music by the king's hired performers
As failure to pay tribute by travelers passing through Babylon
As disregard for the king by officials he had appointed

high-school.explanation: They emphasize the men's royal appointments and tell the king they disregard him by refusing his gods and image.

high-school.question: What opportunity does the king offer before carrying out the penalty?

options.text: Another chance to leave Babylon before the next morning
Another chance to bow when the instruments sound
Another chance to pay money instead of appearing publicly
Another chance to choose which royal god to worship

high-school.explanation: The king offers a renewed opportunity to obey the musical signal and worship, repeating the furnace threat.

high-school.question: How does their reply answer the king's challenge about rescue?

options.text: God will change the image, so they can worship it afterward
God will defeat the army, so they plan an armed rebellion
God must rescue them, so refusal carries no possible danger
God can deliver them, yet obedience does not depend on rescue

high-school.explanation: They affirm that their God can deliver but refuse the king's worship even in the stated alternative, 'if not.'

high-school.question: What immediate effect does their reply have on the king?

options.text: His fury increases, and he intensifies the furnace's heat
His fury increases, and he extends the sentence to their families
His fury increases, and he orders their public execution by sword
His fury increases, and he demands punishment from their provincial governor

high-school.explanation: Nebuchadnezzar becomes furious and orders the furnace heated seven times more than usual.

high-school.question: Which contrast makes the king's observation especially striking?

options.text: They enter alone but are seen leading the royal guards
They enter bound but are seen walking loose without harm
They enter without clothes but are seen wearing royal robes
They enter in secret but are seen speaking to the crowd

high-school.explanation: The text emphasizes their bonds and garments on entry, then the king sees them loose and unharmed with a fourth figure.

high-school.question: How does the king describe the fourth figure in the KJV account?

options.text: As having a form like the Son of God
As having the clothing of the chief priest
As having the weapons of his strongest soldier
As having the face of a former king

high-school.explanation: The KJV records the king's description as 'like the Son of God'; the verse reports his observation.

high-school.question: What does the king do after seeing the men in the fire?

options.text: He withdraws and calls for a second image
He approaches and calls them to come out
He approaches and orders the guards to enter
He withdraws and orders the furnace sealed

high-school.explanation: Nebuchadnezzar comes near, calls them servants of the most high God, and tells them to come forth.

expert.question: What makes the stone's interpretation more than a change in dynasties?

options.text: Its divinely established kingdom neither ends nor transfers to another people
Its divinely established kingdom divides royal offices among successive foreign peoples
Its divinely established kingdom preserves each conquered dynasty under separate rulers
Its divinely established kingdom restores Babylon after the other kingdoms disappear

expert.explanation: The kingdom is not destroyed or left to other people; it consumes the other kingdoms and stands forever.

expert.question: What distinction appears between Nebuchadnezzar's gesture and his verbal acknowledgment?

options.text: He honors Daniel bodily while naming Daniel's God the revealer
He honors his image bodily while naming it the source of wisdom
He honors the astrologers bodily while naming Daniel their chief teacher
He honors Arioch bodily while naming him the discoverer of secrets

expert.explanation: The king falls before Daniel and orders offerings, yet his speech credits Daniel's God with revealing the secret.

expert.question: How does the dedication coordinate worship across the assembled population?

options.text: A sequence of regional summons brings each province forward for worship
A common musical cue triggers the commanded bodily response
A procession of priests leads each official through a spoken royal oath
A series of trumpet calls announces offerings from each gathered nation

expert.explanation: The herald addresses peoples, nations, and languages and links falling down in worship to hearing the instruments.

expert.question: How does royal patronage sharpen the accusation?

options.text: Priests removed from royal office are portrayed as restoring Jerusalem's altar
Captives denied royal office are portrayed as demanding religious privileges
Soldiers promised royal office are portrayed as refusing a military campaign
Recipients of royal office are portrayed as disregarding royal worship

expert.explanation: The accusers stress that the king appointed these men over provincial affairs before charging disobedience.

expert.question: How does the king's renewed offer in Daniel 3:15 combine permission and threat?

options.text: Bowing at the signal is accepted; refusal brings immediate casting into the furnace
Bowing after the feast is accepted; refusal brings removal from the provincial offices
Offering royal tribute is accepted; refusal brings immediate confinement with the palace prisoners
Naming another god is accepted; refusal brings expulsion from the king's gathered officials

expert.explanation: The king offers another chance to bow when the music sounds, but repeats that refusal means the fiery furnace that same hour.

expert.question: Which inference respects both parts of their declaration?

options.text: Confidence in God's power permits worship of the image until danger ends
Confidence in God's power coexists with refusal even under non-deliverance
Confidence in God's power depends on a guarantee that they cannot suffer
Confidence in God's power replaces the need to answer the king's demand

expert.explanation: They say God is able to deliver and then maintain their refusal even under the alternative, 'if not.'

expert.question: What irony accompanies the king's intensified punishment?

options.text: The furnace melts the image being guarded by his assembled officials
The furnace destroys the platform holding his royal guards and counselors
The furnace kills the agents carrying out his urgent command
The furnace burns the offerings being brought by his appointed priests

expert.explanation: His urgency and the furnace's extreme heat kill the men who carry the bound prisoners toward it.

expert.question: What emotional reversal frames the king's actions around the furnace?

options.text: Fear and a bowed head give way to confidence and public celebration
Grief and silent mourning give way to anger and immediate military action
Joy and a shouted command give way to sorrow and private withdrawal
Fury and a changed face give way to astonishment and hurried rising

expert.explanation: His face changes in fury as he orders greater heat; afterward he is astonished and rises in haste on seeing the men in the fire.

expert.question: Which change in royal language accompanies the summons out of the furnace?

options.text: The challenged deliverer becomes a local idol whose priests are called to worship
The challenged deliverer becomes the most high God whose servants are called out
The challenged deliverer becomes a foreign ruler whose ambassadors negotiate the release
The challenged deliverer becomes a royal ancestor whose descendants receive the province

expert.explanation: The earlier challenge asks what god can deliver; now the king calls them servants of the most high God and summons them out.

expert.question: What assurance closes Daniel's interpretation of the stone dream?

options.text: The dream is repeated and its interpretation delayed
The dream is conditional and its interpretation incomplete
The dream is certain and its interpretation sure
The dream is fulfilled and its interpretation forgotten

expert.explanation: Daniel concludes that God has made the future known and affirms the certainty of the dream and surety of its interpretation.
